sections.heading: What is Backtracking?
sections.content: Backtracking builds a solution one choice at a time and abandons (backtracks from) a partial solution as soon as it cannot lead to a valid answer. It explores a tree of decisions using DFS: at each step you choose an option, explore everything that follows, then undo the choice and try the next option. It is the standard way to generate all subsets, permutations and combinations, and to solve constraint puzzles such as N-Queens and Sudoku. The worst case is exponential, so pruning (cutting branches early) is what makes it practical.

sections.heading: When to Use It
items: Generate all subsets, permutations or combinations
Find all solutions, or any one solution, that satisfy constraints
Placement puzzles: N-Queens, Sudoku, word search in a grid
Partition problems: palindrome partitioning, restore IP addresses, split into equal-sum groups
Build strings by rules: generate parentheses, phone letter combinations
Decision at each step has a small number of options and the depth is limited
Keywords: all possible, generate, list every, combinations, permutations, subsets, partition, place, valid arrangement

sections.heading: The Intuition
sections.content: Think of exploring a maze with a ball of string. At every fork you pick a corridor and keep walking. If you hit a dead end, or realize the path cannot reach the exit, you walk back to the last fork (undoing your choices) and take a different corridor. The choose, explore, undo cycle is the heart of backtracking. The set of all possible decision sequences forms a tree, and backtracking walks that tree depth first, cutting off any branch that is already invalid.

How Duplicates and Reuse Change the Code
items: Reuse allowed (Combination Sum): recurse with i
No reuse (subsets, combinations): recurse with i + 1
Input has duplicates and order does not matter: sort, then skip when i > start and nums[i] == nums[i - 1]
Permutations with duplicates: sort, then skip when nums[i] == nums[i - 1] and the earlier twin is not used
Always sort before using the skip rule, since it only compares neighbors

sections.heading: Common Mistakes
items: Adding the same list object to the result instead of a copy (use ArrayList(path)), so every answer ends up empty
Forgetting to undo the choice (removeAt, used[i] = false, restoring the cell) after the recursive call
Using i instead of i + 1 (or the other way around) and producing repeated or missing answers
Not sorting before applying the duplicate-skip rule
Skipping duplicates with i > 0 instead of i > start in subsets and combinations
Forgetting the base case, or checking it after the loop instead of before
Pruning too late, which turns a fast solution into a timeout
Modifying a shared collection while iterating over it
Returning from the base case without recording when the solution is complete

rows.detail: Number of nodes in the decision tree times the work per node, usually exponential or factorial
O(depth) for the recursion stack and the current path, not counting the stored output
Often dominates: 2^n subsets or n! permutations must be written out
Does not change the worst case but often cuts the real running time dramatically
If subproblems repeat, switch to dynamic programming (memoization)

sections.heading: Key Takeaways
items: Backtracking is DFS over a decision tree: choose, explore, unchoose
Always store a copy of the path when you record a solution
Use a start index for subsets and combinations, and a used array (or swaps) for permutations
Sort first and skip equal neighbors to avoid duplicate answers
Prune early with constraints, bounds and symmetry checks to avoid exploring hopeless branches
If the same subproblems keep reappearing, memoize and move to dynamic programming
